paragraphs.heading: What a lens is
paragraphs.text: A lens is a device that lets light through and uses refraction to bring a beam together or spread it apart. A simple lens is one piece of transparent material, while a compound lens is built from several simple lenses, called elements, usually lined up along a shared axis. Lenses are made from materials like glass or plastic and are ground, polished or moulded into shape. Unlike a prism, which bends light without focusing it, a lens can focus light into an image.

paragraphs.heading: Where lenses are used
paragraphs.text: Lenses are used in imaging devices such as telescopes, binoculars and cameras. Glasses use them to correct faults of vision such as myopia and hypermetropia. The name comes from lēns, the Latin word for a lentil, because a lens that bulges on both sides has a lentil's shape. Devices that focus or spread other kinds of waves are called lenses too, including microwave, electron, acoustic and even explosive lenses.

paragraphs.heading: Lenses in the ancient world
paragraphs.text: How far back real lenses go is debated. Some scholars read the archaeological evidence as showing wide use of lenses across several thousand years of antiquity, while others think most ancient examples were decorative, apart from some burning glasses. The Nimrud lens, a piece of rock crystal from the 7th century BCE, may or may not have served as a magnifying glass or a burning glass. The oldest certain mention of a lens used as a burning glass comes in Aristophanes's play The Clouds, from 424 BCE, and Pliny the Elder confirms that the Romans knew of burning glasses.

paragraphs.heading: From reading stones to telescopes
paragraphs.text: Between the 11th and 13th centuries people used reading stones, simple lenses first made by cutting a glass sphere in half. Spectacles were invented in Northern Italy during the later 1200s as an improvement on them. That began an industry of grinding and polishing spectacle lenses, first in Venice and Florence and later in the Netherlands and Germany. Hands-on experiment with lenses in the Dutch spectacle-making centres led to the compound microscope around 1595 and the refracting telescope in 1608.

paragraphs.heading: The colour problem
paragraphs.text: Once telescopes and microscopes existed, people in the 17th and early 18th centuries tried many lens shapes to fix the colour errors they saw. Opticians varied the curvature, wrongly assuming the errors came from defects in the spherical form of the surfaces. Theory and experiment showed instead that no lens made of a single element could bring every colour to one focus. The answer was the compound achromatic lens, invented by Chester Moore Hall in England in 1733 and also claimed by John Dollond in a 1758 patent.

paragraphs.heading: Lens shapes
paragraphs.text: Most lenses are spherical, meaning each of their two surfaces is part of the surface of a sphere. Each surface can be convex, bulging outward, concave, dipping inward, or flat. The line joining the centres of those spheres is the lens axis. Toric lenses instead have two different curvatures in two directions at right angles, so they focus with a different strength along different lines. Eyeglass lenses of this kind are used to correct astigmatism.

paragraphs.heading: The lighthouse lens
paragraphs.text: Growing trade across the Atlantic drove the building of modern lighthouses in the 18th century. To be seen from as far away as possible, an ordinary convex lens would have had to be very large, which made cost, design and building harder. The Fresnel lens met this problem by using less material, divided into concentric rings. It was first fully installed in a lighthouse in 1823.
